title: Everything you need to start drawing, for under $20
excerpt: A pencil, an eraser and cheap paper will take you a long way. Here's the short list, and what to skip.
content:
People put off drawing because they think they need the right kit. You don't. Here's everything on my desk when I teach the first week.

A soft pencil

A 2B pencil makes dark lines and light ones. One is enough; two if you lose things.

A kneaded eraser

It lifts graphite without tearing the paper, and you can shape it to a point for small fixes.

Cheap paper, lots of it

Printer paper is perfect. Expensive sketchbooks make people scared to make mistakes, and mistakes are how you learn.

What to skip for now

Sets of twenty pencils, blending stumps and fancy pens. Add them later if you want them.

Ready to use them? Draw people in 30 days starts with exactly this kit.

title: Why fifteen minutes a day beats a whole Sunday
excerpt: Short, daily practice builds the habit and the skill faster than long sessions you can't keep up. Here's how to fit it in.
content:
Every term I see the same thing: the students who draw a little every day overtake the ones who wait for a free afternoon.

Little and often

Your eye and hand learn by repetition. Fifteen minutes a day is over a hundred hours a year.

Tie it to something you already do

Draw with your morning coffee, on the bus, or while the pasta boils. The habit sticks when it has a place in the day.

Lower the bar

On bad days, draw one cup. One drawing still counts.

Want a nudge? The sketchbook habit gives you a five-minute prompt every day for two weeks.

title: Your first watercolor palette: twelve colors, endless mixes
excerpt: You don't need forty tubes. Twelve well-chosen colors mix almost everything you'll see on a sketching trip.
content:
Most beginner sets are full of colors you'll never use. Here's the palette I carry in my pocket.

Two of each primary

A warm and a cool yellow, red and blue. Between them they mix clean greens, oranges and purples.

Three earth colors

Yellow ochre, burnt sienna and a dark brown for buildings, skin and shadows.

One green and one grey

A green for when you're in a hurry, and a neutral grey for shadows on white walls.

See it in use in Watercolor for sketchers.

title: Three tips for faces that look like people
excerpt: Eyes halfway down, a shorter nose than you think, and the corners of the mouth. Three checks that fix most portraits.
content:
When a face looks wrong, it's usually one of three things.

The eyes are halfway down the head

Almost everyone draws them too high. Measure from the chin to the top of the skull; the eyes sit in the middle.

The nose is shorter than you think

Check it against the space between the eyes and the chin before you draw the details.

The corners of the mouth tell the mood

Turn them up a fraction and the whole face smiles. Leave them flat and it looks bored.

There's much more in Faces and portraits.
